articles.title: Pacientes devem estar atentos a mensagens sobre exames e consultas | G1
articles.standfirst: Sistema do Estado envia mensagens por WhatsApp com orientações sobre marcação de atendimentos. Falta de retorno pode ocasionar cancelamento.
articles.summary: Sistema do Estado envia mensagens por WhatsApp com orientações sobre marcação de atendimentos. Falta de retorno pode ocasionar cancelamento.
articles.body:
Serena, assistente virtual da Saúde, envia mensagens para confirmação e lembrete aos pacientes — Foto: Reprodução

A Prefeitura de Rio das Ostras vem firmando parcerias e reorganizando serviços para dar mais agilidade ao agendamento de exames e consultas. As marcações estão evoluindo e os moradores que estão aguardando devem ficar atentos. No caso de exames e consultas em unidades de saúde fora do Município, os pacientes recebem mensagens, via whatsapp, e devem seguir as orientações, para não perder seu atendimento.

“O trabalho da Prefeitura para reduzir o tempo de espera, especialmente, pelas consultas e exames de média e alta complexidade vem dando resultado. Estamos firmando parcerias e otimizando os sistemas de marcação. No entanto, notamos que os pacientes estavam faltando aos exames e consultas por não atentar para as mensagens enviada pelo Sistema de Regulação. Por isso estamos reforçando essa orientação”, explica a subsecretária de Atenção Especializada em Saúde, Deiva Motta.

COMO FUNCIONA – Pacientes da Rede Municipal de Saúde podem ser encaminhados para exames, consultas e cirurgias em unidades privadas conveniadas fora do Município.

Quando se trata de unidade estadual, o morador é inserido no Sistema Estadual de Regulação (SER).

Assim que o paciente é inserido no SER, a assistente virtual Serena, entra em contato com o morador, via whatsapp, para enviar informações sobre o agendamento, como data, local e horário.

Antes da consulta ou exame, o paciente agendado recebe lembretes para que possa se organizar e não perder a data. Em todas as etapas, é necessário responder às solicitações simples feitas pelo sistema virtual para garantir e confirmar o atendimento.

A confirmação em resposta à mensagem da Serena é fundamental. Sem essa confirmação, o agendamento pode não ser efetivado. O processo é simples e rápido.

Para receber as mensagens com informações sobre marcação de exames, é necessário que o morador mantenha seu telefone atualizado no cadastro do SUS.

ALERTA – Importante esclarecer que as mensagens oficiais nunca solicitam senha, dados bancários ou pagamentos. Caso o morador receba mensagem solicitando senhas ou pagamentos, trata-se de golpe e deve ser denunciado.

articles.title: A&E did not get the basics right - now my son's life is ruined at 32
articles.summary: Oli's experience is one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England, BBC analysis shows.
articles.body:
In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness.

He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, and was sent home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now lives in almost complete paralysis.

Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in emergency departments.

Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history.

Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time.

Stephen says the whole family – including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him.

"The hospital didn't get the basics right and my son has paid a terrible price – it's ruined his life. It was an awful error. He trusted the health service and believed it was there to help him, not destroy him."

He says Oli's body is now twisted and paralysed and he has no ability to move around. His breathing, feeding and toileting are all done through tubes at the neurological rebab centre where he is being cared for. He can only communicate through blinking, but Stephen believes he understands everything going on around him.

"There is no worse space for a human to occupy – it's a permanent living nightmare."

North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Warrington's A&E, has now accepted a breach of duty in not ordering a CT brain scan, which on the balance of probabilities would have identified the fluid build-up in his brain and led to surgery to address it.

In a statement, the trust said: "We are deeply sorry that Mr Coppock did not receive that standard of care that should be expected and we recognise the distress and lasting impact on patients and their families when harm is caused."

An interim damages payment has been agreed. However, Oli's solicitor, Tanzeela Aslam, head of medical negligence at Express Solicitors, says the time taken to get to this point – more than two years – has just added to the failings, depriving him of access to funds for therapies and support that could have improved his quality of life.

"Oli's case illustrates how preventable errors within the NHS can have devastating and life-changing consequences for individuals and their families."

She says she is seeing more and more A&E-related cases – something she too puts down to the growing pressures.

"There has been an increased reliance on corridor care for patients, and we are seeing cases across A &E departments of misdiagnoses that have led to serious injury and in some cases death."

A BBC analysis of NHS Resolution figures using published data and freedom of information requests showed there were more than 1,623 A&E-related clinical negligence claims in 2025-26 in England – up from 1,151 in 2020-21.

It means A&E is now the single biggest area for clinical negligence claims in terms of number. The value of those claims exceeded £550 million last year.

Not all claims will result in damages being paid – that happens in about half of all cases. The NHS sometimes accepts liability but it is judged compensation is not needed.

And there were points during the 2010s when the number of claims were higher per A&E attendance than they were now before falling.

But the sustained increase over the past five years is causing concern, say experts.

The pattern is not being repeated in other areas, such as maternity or orthopaedics, and the low point in 2020-21 is thought to be unrelated to any behaviour changes by patients during the Covid pandemic as it takes three years on average for a claim to be submitted.

The Royal College of Emergency Medicine told the BBC it was worried about the rise, linking it to increasing pressure and long delays being seen in A&E in recent years.

Over the last two years one in 10 patients who attended A&E spent more than 12 hours waiting to be treated or discharged.

RCEM's Dr Adrian Boyle said the figures were "sobering".

"This is a concern. But it is not surprising when you see how busy departments are. People are staying longer and pressure on staffing is increasing."

But he said clinical negligence cases were still relatively rare – happening in only around one in every 17,000 attendances.

NHS Resolution, which supports NHS trusts with clinical negligence claims, said it was taking action on the "high volume" of claims and has published reports to help the NHS learn from mistakes.

Such mistakes include missing the signs of acute deterioration in patients, failing to order the necessary tests and scans and making incorrect diagnoses.

NHS England said there were signs A&E waiting times were improving - and many of these claims related to historic cases a few years old.

Matthew Hopkins, of NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, said health bosses were "making every effort is made to ensure safe, high-quality care, and that lessons are learned when that falls short".

For Stephen, "every waking hour" is spent worrying about his son.

"I know staff are under pressure," he says, "but this is about doing the basics right. They failed Oli."

articles.title: World-first surgery for Chesterfield baby's rare skull condition
articles.summary: Rory, who is now one, had new "super elastic" springs inserted to reshape his skull.
articles.body:
A "happy and cheeky" baby boy with a rare skull condition is doing well a year after becoming the first in the world to be given a new type of treatment.

One-year-old Rory Potter, from Chesterfield in Derbyshire, was diagnosed with severe sagittal craniosynostosis - a condition where the skull fuses before birth - shortly after he was born in April last year.

He underwent surgery in September to have "super elastic" springs inserted, which gradually reshaped his skull before being removed.

His mother Jo Potter said: "You wouldn't know what he's been through."

The 36-year-old described him as "happy, cheeky and full of energy".

"He's just like every little boy and hitting milestones and he will have a great story to tell when he's older."

She added that she and her husband Harry "cannot thank the team enough for the care, compassion and reassurance".

"Not to mention their dedication to medical science to support and help children thrive.

"Throughout the process, every element was explained so well. We knew what was going to happen and how, we received amazing support from each member of the team."

Treatment usually involves skull reshaping surgery, which takes place within the first months of life.

Over the last two decades, this has involved the use of stainless steel springs to gradually widen the gap, giving space for the brain to develop and for new bone to grow.

But now experts have developed new "super elastic" springs using a special metal called nitinol, a nickel and titanium alloy, with Rory the first patient to have them fitted.

Each spring is custom-designed to the patient and their "super elastic properties" allow them to adapt more naturally to a child's growing skull, experts at Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) said.

The springs were developed by experts at GOSH and University College London (UCL).

Once inserted, the springs remain in place for several weeks to months, gradually reshaping the skull before being removed.

The new technology means children can avoid longer and more invasive operations, and it should see a reduction in blood transfusion rates, experts say.

After Rory was referred to GOSH, medics thought he may benefit from the new nitinol springs, instead of the traditional steel springs, because his case was severe.

Professor Owase Jeelani, consultant neurosurgeon at GOSH, who was part of the team who developed the new springs and led the surgery, said: "Traditional stainless-steel springs are very robust, but they don't always allow us to finetune the force on the skull.

"These new nitinol springs give us much greater flexibility and, in some cases, can prevent the need for further surgery.

"This first surgery is important progress for children with craniosynostosis and, so far, we have seen fantastic outcomes."

Professor Silvia Schievano, who led the team of biomedical engineers at UCL, said: "This has been many years in the making, with thousands of hours of necessary research undertaken.

"It is a very proud moment to see this technology used in a child with such a positive result. It uplifts the importance of engineering research and clinical care coming together to develop new technologies for improved healthcare."

The research work behind the operation was funded by Great Ormond Street Hospital Charity and the National Institute for Health and Care Research GOSH Biomedical Research Centre.

articles.title: Mum 'lost trust' in Addenbrooke's after surgeon review
articles.summary: One parent says the number of patients involved in a review is "ridiculous".
articles.body:
A mum whose daughter was among more than 200 patients "harmed" after being operated on by a now-suspended NHS surgeon says she has lost trust in the hospital that treated her.

Of the 209 patients who "experienced harm" under the care of orthopaedic surgeon Kuldeep Stohr at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, 41 were classed as severe and one person died, as first reported by the BBC on Monday.

Lynn, whose 13-year-old daughter Tammy was among the first to receive findings from an independent investigation last year, said the number of patients involved was "ridiculous".

The hospital trust said it was "deeply sorry". Stohr previously said she was fully co-operating with an investigation.

An ongoing review by the Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (CUH) has looked into the care of more than 900 patients so far.

Many of the cases investigated in the review involved children operated on by Stohr.

The figures were published in a report prepared for the trust's board of directors and was published on its website ahead of a meeting on Wednesday.

The trust removed the report after it was contacted by the BBC for comment.

It said a "confidential interim update" was "shared by mistake in our public board papers".

Lynn questioned who had authored the report, "as us relatives don't trust the hospital and what they say now".

"One or two can be classed as a mistake, but this amount – no. It's ridiculous, especially where parents like me have had to see their children go through additional surgery."

Her family's lawyers previously said they had received a written admission of substandard surgery after screws on Tammy's hip joints, meant to improve her mobility, were inserted in the wrong place and did not properly connect to the bone.

Another parent, Natasha, said she was calling for a public inquiry into how children under Stohr's care – including her 19-year-old daughter Neave – came to be harmed.

The trust's final findings are expected to be shared in November. Chief executive Nicola Ayton said it would be shared with patients and their families before it is published.

Elizabeth Maliakal from Hudgell Solicitors, which is representing several families, said she expected the final report to be "damning".

"Some of our clients, who are children, endured major surgery they didn't need, which had no positive impact on their lives, and left them in pain for years afterwards," she said.

"I expect the final report from the trust, once all the findings of the independent review panel are known, to be highly critical, given we already know from those that we represent that fatal harm was caused in at least one case, and many, many more were harmed."

Stohr was suspended by the hospital and has not been at work since March 2024, initially for personal reasons.

Ayton said the trust was "deeply sorry to the patients and families who came to harm or experienced care below the standards they should expect".

"This should never have happened and we are making changes so that something like this could not happen again," she said.

Stohr's legal representatives declined to comment about the new report when approached by the BBC.

articles.title: Isabel Viña, médico y divulgadora de salud: "Los suplementos adaptógenos, son lo que llamo vitaminas antiestrés..."
articles.standfirst: La experta lo mencionó en un podcast
articles.summary: La experta lo mencionó en un podcast
articles.body: El cansancio es un problema de la actualidad, cada vez más creciente, y más difícil de lidiar con él. Muchas veces vamos al médico y creemos que algo van a encontrar para justificar este agotamiento, sin embargo, nos dicen que aparentemente estamos bien. Pero, ¿cómo podemos solucionar este problema? La médico y divulgadora de temas de salud Isabel Viña, comentó en The Wild Project comenta algunos compuestos que pueden ayudarnos. Para la experta, los suplementos adaptógenos, son lo que ella llama vitaminas antiestrés y funcionan. Algunos actúan sobre un neuropéptido, se asocia con una menor ansiedad, menor estrés, mayor dopamina y serotonina. Además, ayudan también a que tu cuerpo produzca proteínas de choque térmico. Todo ello, influye en que, cuando tienes estrés constante, nuestras células se agotan y no funcionan bien. Esto sucede porque han perdido los sistemas de defensa frente a cualquier estímulo externo. Sin embargo, es importante entender que las proteínas de choque térmico actúan protegiendo la célula frente a los estresores. Los adaptógenos, por tanto, favorecen la síntesis de esas proteínas y estimulan la producción de neuropéptido y, finalmente, llevan a que la persona sea más resiliente al estrés. Aunque pueda parecer que esto es una cosa excepcional, según la experta, esto se conoce desde la Segunda Guerra Mundial, e incluso mucho antes. La especialista recomienda cinco suplementos que podrían ayudar a las personas a regular el cansancio siempre que este no surja a partir de un problema de salud subyacente. Uno de ellos es la esquisandra, lejos de ser un medicamento, es un extracto de hierba que se puede encontrar en cualquier herbolario o tienda que distribuya esta clase de productos. El euterococo es una mezcla de extractos de planta que se encapsulan y es otro de los suplementos que recomienda la especialista. Además, la ashwagandha, la raudiola y la L-teanina son otros de los compuestos que también menciona la experta para conseguir el objetivo de encontrarnos menos cansancio. Todo se puede tomar en formato cápsula. El último que cita es el hongo reishi. Todos estos suplementos van bien para regular el estrés y no afectan a las hormonas, es decir, no tienen componente hormonal, sino que actúa por la vía que ha sido afectada por esa alteración.

articles.title: 105-year-old credits ‘the Good Lord’ for her long life: ‘Every day is a blessing’
articles.summary: Blynda Vidock of Baytown, Texas, still lives independently at 105 and credits faith, athletics and eating well for her remarkable longevity.
articles.body: A Texas woman who just turned 105 attributes her long life to "the good Lord." While Blynda Vidock's faith may have played an important role in her longevity, the Baytown resident has also followed many of the habits that experts say can contribute to a longer, healthier life. "The good Lord put me here for so many years, and it’s His life through me," she told FOX 26 Houston at her recent birthday celebration. "But I’ve always been very athletic, played tennis, swam all my life and ate good food." GEORGIA WOMAN CELEBRATES 112TH BIRTHDAY, REVEALS HER SECRET TO A LONG LIFE Vidock joked that she preaches to her children, grandchildren and "great-grands" to eat healthier, but said, "They still eat junk food!" "We live faster nowadays," she said. "We used to have time to sit down and have a meal together." Vidock was born in 1921 and grew up in West Palm Beach, Florida. While working for $15 a week at a bank in West Palm Beach, she crossed paths with big-name movie stars Clark Gable and Fred Astaire, and also recalled encountering a young John F. Kennedy. She met Coast Guardsman Charles "Chuck" Vidock while volunteering with the USO during World War II. The two married and moved to Texas in 1946 and spent decades traveling the world together. LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS Vidock is "completely sharp, independent and full of stories from a century of living," according to the report. A video from her birthday party shows the centenarian walking around and chatting animatedly with the many friends and family members who gathered to honor her. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "It’s wonderful to have you people here, and I don’t know if I’m supposed to dance or sing or get up on the table," she said. "I think I've been made queen for a day, and I've got my 15 minutes of fame, so you better enjoy it because it won't come again." Every morning when she wakes up, Vidock said she wonders, "‘This is another day, Lord, why am I here?’" adding, "Every day is a blessing!" She said "the saddest part about getting old" is watching people lose their mental sharpness, and credits "the good Lord" with allowing her to keep hers. Vidock said a few simple habits have helped her live so long. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Living like you know you’re supposed to live, being kind to people, and everything in moderation helped, and I got blessed with good genes, but then I took care of my body," she said. Expert tips to improve healthspan Dr. Annu Navani, chief medical officer at Le Reve Wellness in San Jose, California, recently told Fox News Digital that longevity medicine is more about adding life to years than adding years to life. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Rather than splurging on costly biohacks, procedures or supplements, Navani recommends focusing on simple daily practices that can enhance quality of life. Getting high-quality sleep — about seven hours a night for the average person — is necessary for people to perform optimally and has been linked to a healthier lifespan, the expert said. Managing stress is another key factor in healthy aging, according to Navani. Regular physical activity and social interaction — two other factors linked to longevity — can also help people keep stress in check, as can regular meditation. Eating a nutritious diet that includes a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, protein and dairy, while limiting added sugars and ultraprocessed foods, is another important component of healthy aging. Longevity experts David Cravit and Larry Wolf, authors of "The SuperAging Workbook," previously told Fox News Digital that maintaining a positive attitude is the No. 1 factor linked to living a longer life. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "People with a positive attitude outlive people with a negative attitude because it reduces stress, which, in turn, reduces inflammation, and inflammation is the cause of most age-related diseases," Cravit said. The authors also recommended setting and working toward new goals, building strong relationships and maintaining a sense of independence as people age. Melissa Rudy and Angelica Stabile of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

articles.title: Forget blackout drinking. Gen Z is throwing 'wellness darties'
articles.summary: A frat threw a "wellness darty." It incited an online debate about the role of Gen Z party culture as more young people look to de-center alcohol.
articles.body:
Running, cold plunges and protein bars might not sound like your typical college party . But at one University of Florida fraternity house last month, they were the main event. Students jogged, stretched and worked out in matching sets before cooling off in ice baths and grabbing fruit.

College kids are calling them "wellness darties," or daytime parties, and the internet has thoughts.

"Imagine explaining a wellness darty to someone who went to college in 2012," Aydan Child, founder of Peak Pulse Run Club, wrote over a Sep. 8 TikTok of University of Florida students working out in front of a frat house. "A little bit of wellness in college won't hurt anyone," reads the caption.

The video, which has racked up 2.6 million views, spurred a larger debate over what party culture looks like for a generation drinking less and increasingly interested in wellness. These "wellness darties," a fusion of a workout, social gathering and party, are one example of the broader shift toward intentional socializing as more young people look to de-center alcohol .

The original video's comment section filled with opinions and prompted reaction videos with thousands of views . "This new generation is so boring," one commenter lamented.

"What happened to drinking Burnettes or Svedka before class as a pregame because you had a party afterwards? What happened to getting blackout drunk? What happened to day drinking?" one Gen Zer, Erika Jensen, posted in response to the original video. "I fear we have lost the plot."

Research has shown young people are indeed drinking less , having less sex and going to fewer parties . While those things can be positive, they're also indicators of increased social isolation. Much of Gen Z missed out on pivotal years in the classroom or office during the COVID-19 pandemic, impacting their ability to socialize.

Simultaneously, Gen Z is prioritizing wellness and longevity more than past generations. Groups like Peak Pulse and Sweat & Soak have tapped into that, and found an interested customer base in Greek life students.

The party that went viral was the innovation of Child, a 25-year-old UF graduate who wanted to provide college students alternative social outings. While Child is sober, he says that the events are intended for everyone. The events frequently end at a bar, where matcha and coffee are encouraged, but alcohol is also offered.

"People are realizing we can have fun in other ways and meet people, get outside, have a good time while feeling good, looking good, and actually bettering ourselves rather than just drinking," Child says.

Still, many young people argue that college party culture is as alive as ever. Florida State University, one of the schools Peak Pulse has partnered with, in August was ranked as Niche's #1 party school.

University of Alabama sophomore Riley Meyer, who helped facilitate a Sweat & Soak darty on Aug. 29, says it feels "really good" to socialize without alcohol.

"I think my generation… does have a problem with socialization, especially without the context of alcohol at a party, and I think that when you have an activity built in, it gives you something to do," Meyer says.

Meyer says the online reaction to the wellness darties is "crazy," and that these videos are just one snippet in the lives of college students, many of whom she says party "90% of the weekend." She says that students will likely begin pregaming at 8 a.m. for the University of Alabama's home opener football game next weekend.

"People are acting like this wellness darty is every single day," Meyer says. "It's more about balance."

They dance at sunrise, then go to work: Inside a sober morning rave in NYC

This union of wellness and party culture is part of a bigger shift toward intentional socializing as more Americans de-center alcohol and seek out offline events. According to data from Eventbrite , morning raves have grown 20%. Coffee clubbing, and sauna and ice bath events, which are also part of this soft clubbing movement, are up 478% and 256%, respectively.

In New York, popular dance club Joyface hosts a matinee disco geared toward millennials. There are variants of cold plunge parties in San Francisco and Savannah , Georgia; a silent disco in Florida ; and coffee parties in Toronto and Miami.

Child and Meyer view these college parties as an extension of that. Wellness and party culture can coexist, they say.

After the wellness darty Meyer attended at the University of Alabama, she says she and her friends went home, took a break, and then went out.

"It's not like it prohibited us from going out, it just gave us something else to do," Meyer says.

A wellness darty is equal parts workout, social gathering and daytime party. They often involve runs, pilates or high-intensity interval training workouts accompanied by cold plunges, energy drinks, coffee and matcha.

articles.title: Drug developed for lung disease may slow biological aging in surprising ‘bonus’
articles.summary: Rentosertib, an AI-discovered drug for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, made patients appear three to four years biologically younger in a clinical trial.
articles.body: A drug being developed to treat a serious lung disease may also help to slow the aging process, researchers say. In a small clinical study, patients who took rentosertib – developed by Insilico Medicine in Massachusetts – showed changes in blood proteins that made them appear biologically younger. Several tests estimated that after treatment, the patients were biologically about three to four years younger. EATING COMMON DAIRY FOOD EVERY DAY MAY SLOW BIOLOGICAL AGING, STUDY SUGGESTS "There is a promising trend in age reversal in addition to treating the disease, and it came as a bonus for disease treatment," first author Alex Zhavoronkov, PhD, founder and co-CEO of Insilico Medicine, told Fox News Digital. "It basically means that you are predicted to be younger using a validated set of aging clocks. We don’t know what that means yet." The results were published in Nature Biotechnology and presented Monday at the Nature conference at Sorbonne University in Paris. ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION The researchers caution, however, that this does not yet prove the drug can actually reverse aging or help people live longer. "It’s early days," Zhavoronkov noted. "The drug is still investigational." What is rentosertib? Rentosertib is an experimental drug, discovered with the help of artificial intelligence, that is being developed to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a serious disease that causes scarring in the lungs. In an unexpected outcome, the drug was found to change patterns of proteins in the blood in ways that made patients appear an average of three to four years younger, in one case up to six years. Six different aging tests showed the same general pattern, with patients who took rentosertib "scoring" biologically younger than those who received a placebo. The strongest effect was seen after four weeks in patients taking 30 mg of the drug twice a day. LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS When researchers compared the results with data from more than 55,000 people in the UK Biobank, they found that the drug changed several blood proteins in the opposite direction from what is normally seen with aging. The researchers also found signs that the drug may affect aging at the cellular level, as it changed processes involved in how cells function and respond to damage. "Everybody agrees that living longer should be a fundamental human right for everyone." Zhavoronkov said the company's approach uses AI to search for what he calls "molecular criminals" — biological targets that may contribute to both aging and disease. The study – which was published in Nature Biotechnology – involved researchers from Insilico Medicine as well as Harvard Medical School, Stanford University, the Broad Institute, RWTH Aachen University, Peking University and Westlake University. Study limitations Zhavoronkov stressed that the findings are preliminary. "This is a pilot," he said. "It is early [and] exploratory." The study had some limitations, including the small sample size – just 42 patients were analyzed over a 12-week period. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The participants all had IPF, which can change many of the same proteins researchers use to measure biological aging. This means it’s possible that the improvements in the participants’ lung disease was related to the changes in blood proteins. The findings don’t prove that the drug actually slows aging, keeps people healthier longer or extends their lives, the researchers acknowledged. The results were based only on changes in proteins in their blood, and do not yet support the use of rentosertib as an anti-aging treatment. Risks and side effects The risks and side effects associated with rentosertib were found to be "manageable," according to Dr. Carol Ann Satler, senior vice president of clinical development for Insilico Medicine. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The most common potential side effects included mild diarrhea, slightly lower potassium levels in the blood and temporary increases in liver enzymes. "Once you stop the drug, essentially, they return to normal," Satler told Fox News Digital. In the next trial, the doctor said, "We'll be looking to adjust the doses of the drug based on the side effect profile so that people can stay on it longer." Looking ahead Rentosertib has now progressed into a year-long phase 3 study of more than 300 patients in China, according to Insilico. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Larger and longer trials – including healthy older adults and populations without IPF – are needed to determine whether the drug truly has anti-aging effects and whether they could lead to better health. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While more research lies ahead, Zhavoronkov said the findings have given him more confidence to continue pursuing drugs that could target both age-related diseases and aging itself. "Everybody agrees that living longer should be a fundamental human right for everyone," he said.

articles.title: Joe Biden shares health update after prostate cancer diagnosis while issuing warning to others
articles.summary: Joe Biden revealed his radiation treatment from last fall "worked as intended" as he urged men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden shared an update on his battle with prostate cancer Tuesday, revealing that radiation treatment he underwent last fall "worked as intended" while urging American men not to delay conversations with their doctors about cancer screening. Biden, 83, issued the update in a lengthy social media post marking Prostate Cancer Awareness Month, saying the occasion was more personal for him following his diagnosis last year. "The radiation treatment from last fall worked as intended, and I continue to do the things I care about, like finishing my memoir," Biden wrote. JILL BIDEN SAYS FORMER PRESIDENT WILL LIVE WITH STAGE 4 CANCER 'FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE,' HAS SLOWED DOWN He also thanked the doctors, nurses and other medical professionals who have treated him, saying their "skill, dedication, and compassion mean so much." Biden used much of the message to urge men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors, pointing to the dramatically higher survival rate when the disease is detected early. CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’ "Talk to your doctors. Ask the hard questions. Do it for yourself, and do it for the people who love you," Biden wrote. Biden said men at average risk should begin discussing prostate cancer screening with their doctors around age 50, while Black men and those with a family history should begin those conversations earlier. SIMPLE SITTING CHANGE LINKED TO LOWER RISK OF CANCER DEATH, STUDY FINDS The American Cancer Society recommends discussing screening at age 50 for average-risk men, age 45 for Black men and certain men with a family history, and age 40 for some men at even higher risk. Biden’s office announced in May 2025 that the former president had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had metastasized to his bones. JOE BIDEN'S CANCER HAS SPREAD FURTHER, LEAVING HIM IN 'VERY PAINFUL' CONDITION, HUNTER REVEALS The diagnosis came after Biden experienced increasing urinary symptoms and doctors discovered a prostate nodule. His office said at the time that the cancer had a Gleason score of 9, Grade Group 5, but was hormone-sensitive, allowing for effective management. Biden later underwent radiation therapy and completed that course of treatment last fall. CANCER SURVIVORS SAW MAJOR IMPROVEMENTS IN SLEEP AND WELL-BEING WITH ONE WEEKLY PRACTICE Fox News Digital reached out to Biden’s office for additional comment on his current health, treatment and prognosis. Biden closed Tuesday's message by thanking those who have continued to pray for him and his family. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It’s my hope and prayer that by sharing our experience and being part of this important conversation, we can help save lives," he wrote. "And no matter what, keep the faith. God bless you."Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price and Robert McGreevy contributed to this reporting.
